item.title: 'Swamp-like colors' on the moon: New 130-page NASA science report reveals strange sights from Artemis II mission - Live Science
item.description:
Quick facts

What it is: A view of the moon from the Artemis II crew

Where it is: Aristarchus Plateau, on the moon's near side

When it was shared: Oct. 8, 2026

What color is the moon? Ask an Earthling, and you'll get a predictably monochromatic answer: white or gray.

But ask the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission — who spent nearly seven hours circling the moon from just 4,000 miles (6,400 kilometers) from the lunar surface this April — and you'll wonder if they're talking about the same dusty satellite we can see from Earth.

Yellow, brown, green, blue and tan features fan across vast volcanic plains and lurk at the edges of ominous craters, according to the crew's in-the-moment observations, which were shared this week in NASA's Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report. The 130-page document catalogs everything crewmembers Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen saw during their historic close flyby of the moon on April 6, drawing from 814 gigabytes of photo, video and audio recordings taken from the Orion crew capsule.

This rainbow of lunar color represents distinct geological features that could inform future missions on where to land and where to explore as the world's space agencies race to set up a permanent presence on the moon.

One spot that particularly enthralled the astronauts (and is featured in the image above) is the Aristarchus Plateau — a broad, elevated region on the northwestern edge of the moon's nearside. The region hosts one of the moon's densest collections of ancient volcanic features, including swaths of dark lava deposits and colorful volcanic glasses.

Koch, mission specialist for Artemis II, was shocked to see distinct yellow shades in the region; she likened the plateau to "a yellow snow-capped mountain," with sunlight-reflecting craters providing the bright "snow." She went on to call the region "a jaundiced cheek of the Moon."

"There are so many colors now," Glover, Artemis II's pilot, added while photographing the area. "There's also a green. I see brown, especially Aristarchus and north toward the north pole. … It kind of flows down from the north in brown streaks."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to the report authors, these colorful hues "could be associated with orange (titanium-rich) and green (magnesium-rich) glass beads respectively," similar to volcanic glass beads collected by the Apollo 15 and 17 missions on separate parts of the moon.

"Chaos across the entire area"

Another colorful patch of the lunar surface that caught the crew's attention was Orientale Basin — a huge, young and multiringed impact crater that's about three times as wide as Massachusetts, according to NASA. Straddling the moon's near and far sides, this massive bull's-eye is rarely visible from Earth, but it dominated the crewmembers' field of view as they orbited around the side of the moon.

"It has just created chaos across that entire area," Wiseman, commander for the mission, said at the time.

This photo, taken by the Orion capsule's external cameras, shows the lunar terminator, where the dayside bleeds into the nightside. Orientale Basin is the large bull's-eye-like feature near the bottom right of the moon.

When flying over this sprawling basin, the crew noted gray, brown, tan and green below. The largest, outermost ring in the basin contained "almost swamp-like colors," Koch reported, while Glover spotted what looked like "dusted peaks" and "white on the very edges of [the mountains], the spines, the ridgebacks." Chains of craters parading away from the impact site looked "like bubbles rising from a team of scuba divers below," Koch added.

While these may sound like off-the-cuff observations, the Artemis II crew spent more than two years training to study and describe the moon's geology. Their regimen included visiting craters on Earth, taking lessons individually and in classrooms, conducting simulated flybys and, according to the report, bringing "self-selected reference materials" into the Orion capsule to read on the way to the moon.

  • Artemis II crew captures rare double auroras on the dark side of Earth as they zoom toward the moon — Space photo of the week
  • NASA just released 12,000 more Artemis II photos ‪—‬ here are a dozen of our favorites

Thanks to this training, the crew's observations provided a wealth of scientific information that no autonomous camera or orbiter could, the report said.

"The Artemis II mission demonstrated the exceptional value of human observation and cognition as scientific assets in planetary exploration," the report authors concluded. "Unlike cameras, which capture isolated moments and often narrow subsets of a scene, human observers continuously interpret their surroundings, integrating realtime visual perception with contextual understanding."

Or, to put that in Glover's more relatable words to mission control, "It's quite a wicked view."

item.description:
If you thought you’d seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission, you’re wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission.

President Donald Trump on Friday used an award ceremony meant to honor NASA’s Artemis II astronauts to tease the creation of what he described as a “U.S. Space Academy” to be built at an as-yet unannounced site.

Trump signed an executive order to “begin the process of creating a new national academy” as he spoke at the Johnson Space Center and said the new institution would be “a big deal” and one day rival the four existing U.S. service academies which train Army, Navy, Air Force and Coast Guard officers.

“So you think of West Point, and you think of Annapolis, and you think of the Air Force Academy, and you think of the Coast Guard Academy. Great, they're all great, but we're going to have now a Space Force. We're going to have an academy for what the people in this room love the most,” Trump said, referencing his audience of NASA employees and astronauts.

“It'll serve both the United States Space Force as well as NASA and the civilian spaceflight industry, and it'll attract, train, and graduate the very best of our nation, and our nation really has to offer.”

Currently, officers who commission into the U.S. Space Force receive undergraduate education at the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, Colorado. It’s unclear whether what Trump announced would be another military-run service academy or some other type of educational institution.

According to the text of the order released by the White House, what Trump signed does not actually establish any new “space academy” but instead creates a presidential commission to study proposals to create what would be “a NASA-led Federal academy dedicated to combining rigorous technical education with leadership development, discipline, and a durable commitment to public service.”

The president’s comments came moments before he awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the quartet of Artemis II who became the first humans to leave Low Earth Orbit since the Nixon administration when they circumnavigated the moon this past April.

In what could have been an awkward geopolitical moment, the first of the four to whom Trump presented the medal was Jeremy Hansen, the Canadian astronaut who became the first non-American to travel to the moon.

Hansen politely stood at attention, a Canadian flag visible on his left sleeve, while Trump hung the medal around his neck.

Trump’s comments and his presentation of awards to the Artemis crew came after he arrived for his remarks nearly a half-hour late. He was already in Houston because he had flown there the previous day to fundraise for scandal-ridden GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

He brought up his new construction project twice more during a visit to NASA’s Mission Control center, telling workers there that he’d “just opened an academy” and shortly after suggesting that he’d be “picking a site very soon.”

“Everybody wants it. Every state is fighting for it,” he said.

Moments later, he told the American crew members aboard the International Space Station that he’d announced a “very special academy ... for what you people do” that would be “at the same level” as the existing military academies.

item.title: Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey - The Guardian
item.description:
The crew of the historic Artemis II lunar flyby mission have earned the US’s top space medal, officials have announced.

Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August, the US space agency Nasa said.

Nasa’s website indicates that only 30 astronauts have gained the honor – among them Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and John Glenn, who was first to orbit Earth and then served four terms in the US Senate.

Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen were selected for the medal, despite its name, by Donald Trump after the Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, recommended them to the president.

The Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for farthest distance traveled from Earth during their 10-day mission, which began on 1 April. They reached 252,756 miles (406,771km) as they swung above the lunar surface, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles as part of US plans to again land on the moon – then eventually reach Mars.

Furthermore, Hansen – who is from Canada – became the first non-US citizen to fly to the moon.

“This was not easy,” Wiseman said to reporters after the Artemis II mission safely ended with a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. “Before you launch, it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth. And when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human, and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.”

The medal ceremony scheduled for Wiseman and his colleagues at the Johnson Space Center in Houston comes four months after Trump hosted the Artemis II crew at the White House. The occasion was marked in part by the president, who turned 80 in June, telling the astronauts: “I would have had no trouble making it – I’m physically very, very good.”

Nasa listed an 11am start time for the ceremony, with a video live stream of the event available at www.nasa.gov/live.

Trump has sought to embrace the Artemis II crew’s achievements despite his administration’s proposal to cut Nasa’s budget by 23%, including a 46% reduction for space science initiatives, for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October. A House commerce, justice and science subcommittee led by Trump’s Republican party responded by advancing its own Nasa budget proposal that would maintain the science projects the president has been aiming to eliminate.

Beside Armstrong and Glenn, previous Congressional Space Medal of Honor recipients include astronauts who were killed in the Apollo I fire as well as the explosions of the Challenger and Columbia space shuttles.

Douglas Hurley and Robert Behnken were the last astronauts to have been chosen for the medal before the Artemis II crew. Hurley and Behnken in 2020 became the first to launch into orbit on a commercial spacecraft, and they accepted the medal in 2023 during Joe Biden’s presidency.

item.title: NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images

NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled around the Moon and back and, along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. NASA is making the full lunar science dataset from their journey available Wednesday to the global science community and the public for further study.

More than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data – some previously unreleased – have been uploaded to NASA’s Planetary Data System, the public archive for NASA’s planetary missions. This data release includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video of the Moon from the crew’s handheld cameras and the Orion spacecraft’s cameras, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of the crew’s scientific observations of the lunar surface, and crew-annotated images.

When combined, the images, audio files, and crew notes from the expedition provide a powerful lunar science dataset ripe for exploration and analysis. This is the first planetary science dataset captured primarily by humans in more than half a century and humanity’s influence on it is clear. Through training in classrooms, simulations, and field environments, NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen developed expertise in lunar geography, geology, and observational best practices. Their quick decisions about observation targets and which images to capture, along with their perceptions of color and dynamic changes, and discussions about the science of the lunar surface and its surroundings complement decades of data from Apollo astronauts and robotic explorers and deepen our understanding of the Moon as NASA prepares for long-term exploration of the lunar surface.

Along with this data, NASA has released the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide. Together, these three publications provide an overview of the Artemis II lunar mission data and activities, and a technical summary of how the science plan was developed and implemented. This information is already helping inform NASA’s exploration plans for Artemis III and beyond.

item.title: Artemis II astronauts receive nation’s highest space honor for their successful moonshot - AP News
item.description:
Artemis II astronauts receive nation’s highest space honor for their successful moonshot

Artemis II astronauts receive nation’s highest space honor for their successful moonshot

The Artemis II astronauts who flew around the moon earlier this year received the nation’s highest space honor on Friday.

President Donald Trump presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the three Americans and one Canadian whose April lunar flyby set a new distance record for humanity.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other dignitaries took part in the packed ceremony at Houston’s Johnson Space Center, home to Mission Control. Trump used the occasion to announce the creation of a U.S. Space Academy for the Space Force as well as NASA and the commercial space community.

“Space is the hot thing,” the president told the crowd, adding that the academy’s location has yet to be determined.

Commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canada’s Jeremy Hansen became the first astronauts to travel to the moon in more than half a century, coming within 4,067 miles (6,545 kilometers) while test-driving NASA’s new Orion capsule. They were the first to launch aboard NASA’s new moon rocket, a 30-story behemoth that had soared only once before from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

While they didn’t stop at the moon, the four set the stage for next year’s Artemis III docking rehearsal in orbit around Earth. Artemis IV’s moon landing by two astronauts, near the lunar south pole, could follow as soon as 2028.

Trump said Americans will land back on the moon before his term ends. Mars is next — “very shortly,” he said.

The president called the newest recipients “four intrepid space heroes.” He pointed out that they did not do it alone, thanking all who contributed to the Artemis II mission.

“There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars,” Isaacman added.

Wiseman and his crew are in good company, with only 30 astronauts receiving the prestigious honor before them. Many of the recipients were honored posthumously following their tragic spaceflight-related deaths.

Apollo 11 commander Neil Armstrong — whose phrase “That’s one step for man, one giant leap for mankind” gripped the world on July 20, 1969 — was the first to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.

President Jimmy Carter awarded six of these medals in 1978, which also went to Alan Shepard, the first American in space; John Glenn, the first American in orbit; and Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, whose 1968 mission marked humanity’s first lunar voyage.

The most recent recipients were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, the first astronauts to launch aboard a SpaceX rocket. Coming nine years after the space shuttle program’s close, their 2020 test flight to the International Space Station restored America’s ability to launch crews from home soil. President Joe Biden awarded them the medals in 2023.

Dozens of astronauts participated in the ceremony, including Apollo 17 moonwalker Harrison Schmitt, who is now 91, and the four men assigned to NASA’s upcoming Artemis III mission.

Schmitt noted that his mission — Apollo’s last moonshot — was the most productive lunar exploration yet.

“Soon to be surpassed by Artemis,” he said of active astronauts standing behind him.

NASA plans a sustainable moon base staffed by astronauts and robots near the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are thought to hold tons of frozen water that could be turned into rocket fuel and drinking water. China is eyeing the same region.

“The second space race has begun,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matthew Anderson.

As the two-hour ceremony came to a close, the Artemis II astronauts presented Trump with his own blue flight jacket complete with space patches, a promise they made while visiting him in the Oval Office following their mission.

The president then hustled over to Mission Control to call the three U.S. astronauts aboard the International Space Station. He informed them of the new U.S. Space Academy, then briefly handed the phone to two of their spouses for a quick hello.

item.title: 'Dude! No way!' Scientists jump for joy over Artemis II moon science results - Space
item.description:
We have our first look at the science from Artemis II, and it's as amazing as we might have hoped.

This past April, four astronauts strapped in for a flyby around the moon and back to Earth. The first mission to the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972, this success marked an incredible historic milestone. The Artemis II crew also conducted groundbreaking science, observing parts of the moon no human had ever laid eyes on before. And now, we have our first look at some of the science from the mission.

"It's the science community's job now to take these data and go do magical things with it," David Hollibaugh Baker, a member of the Artemis II Lunar Science Team, said during a Wednesday (10/7) press conference that announced the mission's initial science results.

This is just the first batch of data from the mission, but it includes a whopping 996 new images, 814 GB of observations and 521 minutes of audio from the crew that has never been heard before. Everything from that astronauts' handwritten notes and drawings to photographs and verbal observations have revealed exciting new information — about impact flashes on the moon, for example, as well as the terminator line between the lunar "day" and "night" sides and a whole range of lunar colors and observations from beyond the mysterious far side.

Let's take a quick look at some of the highlights.

Impact flashes

"Dude, no way!" Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman of NASA exclaimed in newly released mission audio.

"It's just like a 'bloop!'" mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency added as the flashes appeared on the lunar surface. .

As Artemis II's Orion capsule flew by the moon, the four astronauts onboard — Wiseman, Hansen and NASA astronauts Victor Glover (mission pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist)— started seeing flashes of light on the lunar surface. These were impact flashes caused by small rocks hitting the lunar surface and vaporizing in the impact.

"We have seen three impact flashes so far," Wiseman said to Mission Control at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. "It was not sun glint off a particulate from the thrusters or the purge tanks. It was definitely impact flashes on the moon."

"Amazing news," Mission Control responded. "I literally just looked over at the SER [Science Evaluation Room], and they were jumping up and down, literally."

In total, the crew saw five impact flashes on the moon's surface, which the mission's science team was able to confirm didn't come from other sources.

While the Artemis II crew was equipped with cameras, they were also trained to make observations with the unaided eye. And impact flashes happen too quickly to photograph them, so — as you can see above — the crew used a tablet to make annotations and describe their observations.

"We wanted them to look visually, so there are not camera images of that, but we have their annotations of when they saw them," Jennifer Heldmen, science theme lead for the Artemis II mission, said during the briefing.

A rainbow moon

In addition to seeing impact flashes across the lunar surface, the Artemis II crew observed a wide range of colors on the moon.

Looking up in the night sky, it might seem that the moon is just shades of gray. But as the astronauts saw during their flyby, the moon is gray, black, brown, tan, white, green and even blue. This muted rainbow of colors was not only visually striking, as the astronauts' photos show, but it can also help scientists determine what types of rocks and minerals might be found in different regions across the moon's surface.

"The crew reported greens and yellowish hues on top of Aristarchus Plateau, signaling they were seeing remnants of different styles and epochs of volcanic activity, and the crew contrasted those colors to nearby browns and grays of adjacent volcanic plains," Ariel Deutsch, a member of the Artemis II Lunar Science Team, said during the briefing, givingone example of these colorful observations.

"To me, it's primarily like a brownish-green glass, and then if I went up into the mares [dark volcanic deposits] to the north of Aristarchus, I would give that a very muted brown," Wiseman said in mission recordings shared in this release.

"It's like a jaundiced cheek of the moon," Koch remarked in mission audio, describing yellowish colors on the moon.

And while the crew took some amazing photographs of the moon, in this data release we can also see their handwritten notes annotating the colors they saw on the moon.

The far side of the moon

As the moon is tidally locked to Earth, it has one "day side" that always faces us and one far or "night side" that is always facing away. When the Artemis II astronauts flew by the moon, they flew around the entire object, even around the far side. During their flyby, they were able to see a part of the far sidethat has never been observed up close like this before.

"The Artemis II crew were the first people to see this section of the moon illuminated in all of human history," Alex Stoken, a member of the Crew Lunar Observations team, said during the briefing.

When they approached the moon's far side, the crew also came upon the terminator line, or the boundary between the day and night sides of the moon.

At the terminator, the team was able to view the incredible contrasting shadows and textures of the lunar surface, revealing sharp details about the moon's topography.

"The terminator is the most striking thing that I’ve seen so far," Glover said as the crew flew by.

As they rounded the moon's far side, the moon was backlit by the sun, essentially eclipsing it. This allowed for incredibly unique and sharp views of the moon.

"You’ve got to be kidding me," Koch said in the capsule. "You can actually see mountains."

These are just a few highlights from this incredibly thorough and detailed data release. As we dig deeper into this initial science, you can take a dive through the data yourself here and here.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. item.title: See more sights and sounds from the Artemis II moon mission - Scientific American
item.description:
NASA’s Artemis II mission—a slingshot around the moon earlier this year that sent four astronauts to lunar space for the first time in more than half a century—was an unequivocal success. The voyage was chiefly a technological stepping stone for future crewed forays to the lunar surface, which should culminate with the founding of a small base near the moon’s south pole. But it was also a chance to carry out novel observations of the lunar farside, a largely mysterious realm that has been rarely glimpsed by human eyes.

Although Artemis II’s Orion spacecraft carried minimal science payloads, its astronauts were equipped with digital cameras (and iPhones)—and between April 1 and 10, they captured 814 gigabytes of lunar science data. At a press conference yesterday NASA presented its preliminary findings, which touch on everything from the moon’s surprisingly colorful craters to a series of curious flashes that the astronauts spied in lunar shadows. The release also includes more than eight hours of audio from the crew, videos of their nail-biting return to Earth, hand-annotated images, and much more—all available in a vast online repository.

Besides being breathtaking, the mission’s high-resolution imagery helps address more pragmatic queries: Which landing sites might be best for upcoming missions, and how safe would an outpost somewhere on the lunar farside be? “These findings are going to help shape future Artemis mission architectures,” said Marie Henderson, Artemis II’s deputy lunar science lead, during the press conference.

On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The crew’s sojourn around the moon may have been brief—just under seven hours—but they still surveyed a large swath of the farside, some of which was cloaked in total darkness. Arguably, the mission’s most important discovery emerged from those shadowy regions: five flashes of light, each in a different location on the lunar farside.

These were meteorite impacts. That isn’t inherently surprising: the airless moon gets bombarded by cosmic debris all the time. Sometimes these impactors—either asteroids or cometary fragments—are relatively big: in the spring of 2024, for example, a 15-meter object slammed into the moon with the force of an atomic bomb, cutting out a 222-meter-long pit.

Mostly, though, the moon is pelted by meteoroids the size of bullets or footballs. Each could, with a direct strike, kill an astronaut or trash a fancy new moon rover, so it’s good to know how often these small-but-lethal space rocks rain down on the lunar surface.

That’s why understanding what the Artemis II crew saw on the farside “matters for the future of human exploration,” said Jen Heldmann, a member of Artemis II’s lunar science team and deputy project scientist for Artemis IV, at the press event. Based on the brightness and brevity of the five flashes, scientists think each meteoroid was around 8.5 grams in mass—about as much as two dice. That may seem harmless, but they were moving at tens of kilometers per second, so these impactors are akin to space bullets.

The Artemis II crew flew outside any major annual meteoroid streams, meaning the five impacts they saw in just under an hour likely represent the typical background rate of small meteorite impacts on the lunar surface. With that in mind, NASA gauged the likelihood for a similar space bullet striking a future moon base: about a one-in-10,000 chance per decade. “We’re probably safe going forward,” Heldmann said.

The astronauts were also on the lookout for swarms of lunar dust. This jagged microscopic debris, easily dispersed by meteorite impacts and rocket exhaust, is corrosive, abrasive and adhesive. It makes quick work of wires, space suits and other hardware, chewing through them like space piranhas. Everyone hates it; it’s a major long-term hazard.

During the Apollo moon missions of the 1960s and 1970s, astronauts occasionally reported seeing hazes of sunlight-lofted dust drifting over parts of the lunar surface. But the Artemis II crew didn’t see any, suggesting that this strange phenomenon may be a transient problem rather than a persistent one.

The Artemis II images also revealed the subtle colors of lunar geology, showing that the moon’s seemingly monochrome surface is actually dappled with greens, yellows, grays and browns. Each of these hues, NASA’s analysis confirms, correspond to different types of ancient volcanism, from glasslike oozes to rubbly pyroclastic flow deposits. NASA also hoped that the crew could spy tectonic landforms during their flyby—things like faults, including those that could rupture and create prolonged, and potentially structure-toppling, moonquakes.

At one point, the crew caught a surreal series of arching crevasses in Oceanus Procellarum (the “Ocean of Storms,” a huge basin filled with primeval lava). These were wrinkle ridges, thought to form when the weight of the erupted lava squashes down on the moon’s crust, causing it to snap and contract. “The fact that they were able to see that from orbit was pretty phenomenal,” says Debra Needham, a member of the Artemis II science operations team.

Despite the fanfare of an official press conference, in truth, nothing in NASA’s report is especially revelatory. If anything, it serves as a reminder that unlocking the moon’s secrets—its alien geology, its hazardous landscapes and any scientific or economic treasures it may hold—relies getting a closer, surface-level look via more crewed and robotic investigations. In late September NASA also announced three new science payloads for near-future landings, all building on Artemis II’s success and adding to the case for an eventual moon base. One will monitor micrometeor impacts and other environmental threats at the lunar south pole, a second will search for hollow “lava tubes” that could be sites for underground habitats and a third will study how water ice might accumulate in and change the stability of lunar soil.

The report’s emphasis on future exploration was also tempered by an intentional callback to the past. NASA officials noted that their report’s release date, October 7, has significance in spaceflight history: on this day, back in 1959, the Soviet Union’s Luna 3 space probe beamed back the first-ever images of the moon’s farside, showing it to be a heavily scarred, crater-filled wasteland.

Luna 3’s images were eye-opening but still blandly colorless and fuzzy—especially compared with the kaleidoscopic, panchromatic views from Artemis II’s lunar pirouette. The alluring vistas the astronauts captured on digital cameras and iPhones helped ensure that “the entire world was united around our mission, and our crew,” says Kelsey Young, Artemis II’s lunar science lead. If NASA sticks to its plan and voyages to the moon become commonplace, then extraordinary images like these will quickly become glorious in their ordinariness.

Trump establishes US space academy as Artemis II crew receives Space Medal of Honor

Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen were honored.

President Donald Trump on Friday bestowed the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on the Artemis II crew, marking their historic achievement during a ceremony at Johnson Space Center in Houston.

The crew -- NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen -- traveled farther into deep space than anyone else in history during their trip around the Moon in April. What they learned during their test flight will help NASA return astronauts to the lunar surface as early as 2028.

"We gather here on these storied grounds to celebrate the immense courage and service of four intrepid space heroes whose sense of daring and adventure led them further from Earth than anyone has ever traveled before," Trump said.

Joined at the event by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, the president told a story about being in an important meeting with "the biggest people in the country, maybe some of the biggest people in the world" when someone asked to watch the Artemis II mission.

"You would, really? Right in the middle of our meeting. You want to watch?" Trump recalled saying at the time. He said they had a television set pulled up for the group to watch, adding that "everybody was spellbound."

The president used Friday's occasion to sign an executive order establishing the U.S. Space Academy, a national academy similar to the service academies for the armed forces, such as West Point and the Air Force Academy.

"It will serve both the United States Space Force as well as NASA and the civilian spaceflight industry, and it'll attract, train and graduate the very best of our nation," Trump said.

A location for the new academy will be chosen shortly, according to the president.

During the ceremony, the president personally placed the medal around the necks of each astronaut as they were recognized for their work during the mission.

After receiving his medal, an emotional Wiseman, the commander of the Artemis II mission, spoke about the scale of the joint effort the mission required.

"We wear these four medals, and we are going to wear them with pride. But please know, it is not pride for ourselves that we feel, and I truly mean that," he said. "It is pride for the grit that our families had when we left this planet. It is pride for that team, this NASA team, that sent us on this mission. And it is pride for the international community that stood alongside us, got this vehicle ready, operated and cheered us on."

Glover, the Artemis II pilot, then presented Trump with an official NASA blue flight jacket, saying the crew wanted to make good on its promise to him when they were in the Oval Office.

"To the Artemis crew II, you stand here incredibly deserving of this recognition. Thank you for showing us the moon again, for showing the world your humanity and for passing your knowledge and the baton to the astronauts who will follow in your very accomplished footsteps. There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars," NASA's Isaacman said during the event.

With NASA's astronaut corps seated on stage, Apollo 17 astronaut and former Sen. Harrison Schmitt, a Republican from New Mexico, kicked off the event by speaking about his 1972 mission -- the last mission of the Apollo program.

"Apollo 17's success, as the success of all the other missions was owed to the patriotic dedication, the courage, the competence of young men and women, young men and women, who designed and built and managed and trained and planned each of the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions. It was an extraordinary privilege for me to be part of that."

NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said Apollo pioneers like Schmitt "handed the baton" to the men and women working on the space shuttle program, which built the International Space Station.

"Early this year, the Artemis II crew added their names to that history. They carried humanity around the world, around the moon, for the first time in more than 50 years. Demonstrated that America is ready to return and paved the way for those who will follow," Anderson said.

He also spoke about what's at stake for NASA and the U.S. space program in the years to come.

"The second space race has begun, and right now, America is on the shot clock. Our national security, the prestige of our nation and the dreams of millions of Americans are riding on our ability to get the job done."

Congress authorized the granting of the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in 1969, proclaiming that "The President may award, and present in the name of Congress, a medal of appropriate design, which shall be known as the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, to any astronaut who in the performance of his duties has distinguished himself by exceptionally meritorious efforts and contributions to the welfare of the Nation and of mankind."

Since then, only 34 astronauts have received the honor, including the Artemis II crew. The first recipients of the award in 1978 included Neil Armstrong, Frank Borman, Pete Conrad, John Glenn, Virgil "Gus" Grissom and Alan Shepard.

item.title: Artemis II astronauts saw the flashes of 5 meteor impacts on the moon - Mashable
item.description:
The astronauts who swung around the moon aboard NASA's Orion capsule spotted five tiny sparks from space rocks slamming into the lunar surface, likely the faintest impact flashes humans have ever seen. 

The Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman caught the first one during the mission just six months ago. 

"I just saw a flash, 100 percent," he called out, placing it at about the 7 or 8 o'clock position on the moon. Moments later, he and crewmate Jeremy Hansen both saw another. Hansen described a "pinprick" of light on the lower third of the moon.

You May Also Like

"It's just like a bloop," Hansen said.

Those sightings stunned the mission control room back in Houston, literally causing Kelsey Young's jaw to drop. Young, the mission's lunar science operations lead, admitted she hadn't expected the crew to see any micrometeorites at all. Artemis II flew during a quiet stretch of the year, outside any major meteor shower. 

"You probably saw the surprise and shock on my face," she later told reporters, who had watched a broadcast of the space-to-ground communications. "And though I was not in the science evaluation room, I heard that there were audible screams of delight."

Each flash tells scientists something about how often bits of comets and asteroids pummel the moon and where they hit. NASA wants those numbers before it sends astronauts to live and work there. Lori Glaze, a senior NASA official, said the agency will use such data to judge the risk that meteorites, even the tiniest of space rocks, pose to future moon bases. 

A flash happens when a speeding space pebble smacks the moon. Because the moon has no oxygen, a strike doesn't create combustion fire. Instead, the burst of light comes from the rock's pure kinetic energy.

During the crash, the extreme force instantly vaporizes the rock and a small amount of the moon's surface. That causes a split-second plasma cloud to glow just before cooling in the vacuum of space.

The naked-eye observation of impact flashes during the Artemis II mission, published this week in the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, lends credibility to earlier astronaut reports. Crews reported three such flashes from lunar orbit a half-century ago — one on Apollo 16 and two on Apollo 17. Telescopes on Earth have since logged over 400.

NASA timed the Artemis crew's watch for when the moon blocked the sun from Orion's view. That darkness let the astronauts' eyes adjust enough to catch faint flickers. The moon's surface stayed dark except for a soft glow of sunlight bouncing off Earth.

All five flashes the Artemis astronauts saw happened on the moon's unlit side. None showed any color, and each vanished instantly. Based on how faint they looked, scientists think rocks only a few centimeters across may have caused them, perhaps the size of a grape or a walnut. The crew, which included Victor Glover and Christina Hammock Koch, sketched each location on a tablet while their memories were fresh. 

The moonbound crew saw more but said they reported only the ones that clearly differed from look-alikes. Astronauts often see random bright flashes of light in space — even with their eyes closed — because of cosmic rays passing through the spacecraft and directly striking their optic nerves.

But because some of these flashes were seen by more than one pair of eyes, NASA feels confident in the anecdotal reports.

"It was not sunglint off of particulate from the thrusters or the purge tanks," Wiseman said. "It was definitely impact flashes on the moon."

Meanwhile, the machines got nothing. A camera on the outside of the capsule filmed about two minutes of the eclipse at 30 frames per second and caught no flashes. NASA also hoped its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, a probe that has mapped the moon since 2009, could photograph the sites. The team concluded the craters are probably too small for the camera to see. 

NASA's lunar science team recruited stargazing groups to film the moon through tracking telescopes during the flyby and upload the video to a shared database. But the moon's phase seemed to work against them. Earth-based observers need a dark slice of moon to record flashes. So far, no one on the ground has confirmed one of the flashes from the flyby.

The sightings paid off a bet NASA's science team placed long before launch. Planners carved out dedicated time for the crew to watch for flashes, and the team trained the astronauts to report any they might see at any point in the mission. 

"This is absolutely everything we hoped for by integrating science into flight operations," Young said.

item.title: NASA Just Made Nearly 1 TB of Artemis II Data Available to the Public - WIRED
item.description:
NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.

The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.

In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.

Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.

For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.

For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.

Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.

The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

item.title: NASA shares Artemis II astronauts’ handwritten mission notes - Popular Science
item.description:
Successfully sending Artemis II astronauts on their historic lunar flyby earlier this year required some of the latest and most precise technologies, but not everything in this mission needed the same intense equipment. As crewmates gazed through Orion’s capsule window at the moon’s eclipse of the sun on April 6, 2026, three of the travelers needed a way to easily sketch some of their preliminary observations. They took turns writing their notes on a shared tablet PC—and NASA has recently highlighted their work with a screenshot of their efforts.

Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen had a lengthy list of tasks during their 10-day, 700,000-mile roundtrip. One of the most visually dramatic jobs involved carefully assessing lunar activity while passing across the moon’s dark side from a distance of about 46,000 miles away. The roughly hour-long observation period provided astronauts with an unprecedented opportunity to record meteorite activity.

A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet. Credit: NASA

The tablet screenshot includes notes taken by Wisemen (in blue), Hansen (in red), and Glover (in green) during the moon’s eclipse of the sun. The crew collectively spotted at least five faint flashes of light caused by impacts. According to Wiseman, the first three impacts occurred within about 10 minutes into their observations, while another two happened later during the flyby. Impacts two and four were likely also corroborated by Hansen and Glover.

Since the moon does not have an atmosphere like Earth’s, the lunar surface is regularly bombarded by space rocks. Most of them are comparatively small, but they will still pose a problem for future crewed trips to the surface,especially those stationed in a planned permanent lunar base. The data gathered by Artemis II on April 6 will help NASA better understand these dynamics, and plan for the safest environments possible for their astronauts.

Artemis II’s astronauts safely returned to Earth during a splashdown off the coast of San Diego at 8:07 p.m. EDT on April 11. If all goes as planned, Artemis III’s crew will launch on their mission no earlier than June 2027.

item.title: New videos of NASA's Artemis II launch show the absolute power of the SLS rocket - Space
item.description:
In case you are feeling the empty hole of moon missions, void since the return of the Artemis II astronauts from their trip around the lunar far side six months ago, NASA has you covered.

The agency's Space Launch System (SLS) rocket launched Artemis II on April 1, carrying a crew of four on the first mission around the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972. SLS lifted off from Launch Complex-39B at NASA's Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida, and, to the awe of hundreds of thousands, climbed a bright blue early evening sky on a trail of smoke left by the vehicle's solid rocket boosters up into space.

More than 300,000 people traveled to the Space Coast to watch the launch from dozens of locations around KSC and surrounding cities. But the best views wouldn't be seen until well after the rocket cleared the pad, when NASA technicians recovered the slew of engineering footage captured by dozens of specialized cameras distributed everywhere from the base of the launch pad to drones positioned in the air to track every detail of the launch. Now, NASA has released that footage to the public.

The newly-released videos include a wide spectrum (literally) of views and angles that follow SLS from just before engine ignition through solid rocket booster separation as the rocket leaves Earth's atmosphere. NASA teams used scientifically calibrated in-flight imaging (SCIFLI) to compile footage ranging from the visible light spectrum, to short-wave infrared (SWIR), near-infrared (NIR), mid-wave infrared (MWIR) and infrared — to give you a few helpful acronyms for context as you pursue these videos on NASA's Artemis II album. These different wavelengths of light captured views imperceivable to the eye and typical camera sensors, and allowed NASA technicians to filter out things like the extreme brightness of the flames from the rocket’s engines.

Artemis II was the first crewed mission of NASA's Artemis program, which aims to establish a permanent base on the surface of the moon in the 2030s. It was also the first flight of NASA's Orion spacecraft with astronauts aboard. Essentially a shakedown cruise for Orion's life support systems, the mission flew NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, as well as Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen on a 10-day flight around the moon and back to Earth.

The next mission in NASA's lunar line up, Artemis III, will last longer, but won't fly as far. Artemis III is scheduled to launch in mid-2027 with NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andrew Douglas, as well as European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Luca Parmitano of Italy. They will launch aboard Orion to Earth orbit, where their spacecraft will rendezvous with the two commercial lunar landers NASA has contracted for the Artemis program, SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

Artemis III is expected to last about two weeks as Orion will rendezvous and dock with each lander separately to test the spacecrafts' interoperability. That mission will serve as a precursor to the program's first actual lunar landing with astronauts on Artemis IV, which NASA is targeting to lift off in 2028.

Josh has covered the evolution of NASA's Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon, commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions from the Space Coast, NASA science missions and more. NASA releases Artemis II Moon images: Why the lunar surface is not just grey

The Moon may look grey from Earth, but Artemis II astronauts observed a wider range of colours on its surface.

The Moon may appear grey when we look up at it from Earth, but astronauts on NASA’s Artemis II mission observed a wider range of colours on its surface. NASA has now released thousands of images and hours of recordings from the mission, offering a closer look at what the crew saw during its journey around the Moon.

NASA releases more than 11,000 lunar images

According to NASA’s official website, the space agency has made more than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data available to the public and scientific community. The release includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of astronauts discussing their observations, and images annotated by the crew.

NASA said the material would support further research and help inform plans for future Artemis missions.

Why does the Moon look more colourful than we think?

The Moon is often seen as a grey body in the night sky, but its surface can show subtle shades of brown, tan, green, yellow and blue under certain lighting and viewing conditions. These colours can be difficult to notice in ordinary photographs, particularly when images are processed to highlight surface features or when the Moon is viewed from a distance.

The colours are not simply a visual effect. They can offer clues about the minerals and rocks present on the lunar surface, as well as the Moon’s volcanic past. Different materials reflect sunlight differently, creating variations in colour that scientists can study to learn more about how the surface formed and changed over time.

During Artemis II, the crew reported green and yellowish hues around the Aristarchus Plateau, alongside browns and greys in nearby volcanic plains. For the mission-specific observations and images, see NASA’s official Artemis II data release.

How Artemis II observations could help future missions

The newly released data provides researchers with photographs as well as the astronauts’ spoken observations and annotations. Combining these records can help scientists understand what the crew noticed in real time and compare their descriptions with images of the lunar surface.

The images will help NASA prepare for future lunar missions. They also offer a closer look at the Moon’s surface, revealing details and colours that are difficult to see from Earth.

item.title: NASA Confirms Artemis II Astronauts Saw Rocks Strike the Moon with Their Own Eyes as Full Lunar Dataset Goes Public - Nature World News
item.description:
NASA has confirmed that Artemis II astronauts saw five faint flashes of light from rocks striking the Moon with their own eyes during their April flyby, after ruling out cosmic rays and reflections from the spacecraft as the source. The confirmation appears in the agency's Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, released Wednesday, Oct. 7, alongside more than 800 gigabytes of mission data.

Based on the brightness of the flashes, scientists estimate each incoming rock was no more than a couple of inches wide — about pebble size — but was traveling thousands of miles per hour. NASA said the crew likely caught the faintest lunar impact flashes ever seen with the unaided eye.

The finding matters beyond the spectacle. NASA says understanding how often small rocks hit the Moon is essential for assessing long-term risks to future lunar habitats and infrastructure, as the agency plans Artemis III and longer human stays on the lunar surface.

Five Pinpricks of Light From 46,000 Miles Away

The flashes came during a 54-minute total solar eclipse as the Orion spacecraft passed behind the Moon on April 6, a period when the crew was out of contact with Earth. With the Sun blocked, the dark lunar disk made extremely faint bursts easier to spot. Orion was about 46,000 miles from the Moon at the time.

Three crew members marked flashes on a tablet image of the eclipsed Moon: NASA commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen. Their notes indicate several circled marks were likely the same impacts seen by more than one person. Crew audio released by NASA captures one astronaut reacting with "Dude! No way!" as the flashes appeared.

Lunar scientists had asked the crew, which also included mission specialist Christina Koch, to watch for impact flashes as part of the science plan. Even so, NASA said some scientists were astonished when the astronauts reported seeing them. Apollo crews reported similar flashes from lunar orbit decades ago.

An Evidence Check on the Sightings

The report is a preliminary summary of crew observations reviewed by NASA's science team, not a peer-reviewed study. Early public accounts in April counted as many as six flashes, according to Sky & Telescope, while NASA's report settled on five after checking each sighting. The size estimates come from the brightness of the flashes, not from recovered material.

Independent scientists said in April that the sightings raised useful questions. Peter Schultz, a professor emeritus of geological sciences at Brown University, told AFP the observations show the "daily flux of meteors should be monitored more closely" before a lunar base is built, according to The Standard. Bruce Betts, chief scientist at the Planetary Society, said at the time he was surprised the crew saw so many and that their descriptions could help estimate both impact frequency and projectile size.

Five flashes during one eclipse cannot establish an impact rate on their own. Ground telescopes have confirmed well over 400 lunar impact flashes since 1999, Sky & Telescope reported, and the Artemis II observations add a rare human-eye view of the far side to that larger record.

Small Impacts, Big Questions for a Moon Base

The Moon has no atmosphere to slow or burn up incoming debris, so even pebble-sized rocks strike the surface at full speed. Pinning down how often that happens helps engineers decide how much shielding habitats, rovers and solar arrays will need over years of use.

The report also documents other observations. Crew members described subtle grays, browns, tans, greens and blues across the lunar surface, colors that hint at titanium-rich volcanic rock, varying iron content and glass formed by eruptions or impacts. They studied the terminator, the boundary between lunar day and night, because its low-angle light resembles conditions near the Moon's south pole, where future Artemis crews are expected to land.

Earth scientists found value in the record as well. A full-disk nighttime image of Earth taken on the mission's second day captured auroras at both poles, active weather systems, lightning over central Africa and a large Saharan dust plume drifting westward, according to NASA. Satellites usually capture the planet in narrow strips, making a whole-Earth view at night unusual.

800 Gigabytes Now Open to the Public

NASA uploaded the full lunar science dataset to its Planetary Data System archive, including more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video clips, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of the crew's observations and crew-annotated images. Some of the material had not been released before, the agency said in its data release announcement.

NASA also published a lunar science operations report and a data user guide explaining how the science plan was built and carried out. The agency said the information is already shaping plans for Artemis III, and that accessible versions of the full reports are still in progress.

Lunar impact flashes pose no danger to people on Earth — and anyone can help study them. Readers who want to take part can join NASA's Impact Flash citizen science project, which asks amateur astronomers with telescopes to record the Moon's unlit side and help build a global record of impacts. Any reports should go through the project rather than social media, since short-lived glints can come from satellites, aircraft or camera artifacts.

Researchers worldwide can now compare the crew's descriptions with images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, which has mapped the Moon for years. Those comparisons will show how human perception of color and brightness lines up with instrument data, a key question as astronauts take on more science on the surface.

The bottom line is that NASA has now formally confirmed a rare naked-eye sighting of rocks hitting the Moon, and the evidence is public for anyone to examine. The sample is small, and the impact estimates remain preliminary. The next step is analysis by outside scientists, which will help determine how the observations feed into safety planning for crews who will live on the Moon rather than just fly past it.

What Readers Want to Know

What did the Artemis II astronauts see?

They saw five extremely faint flashes of light on the Moon's darkened surface, caused by small rocks striking it at high speed, during a total solar eclipse on April 6.

How did NASA confirm the flashes were real?

NASA's science team ruled out other explanations, including cosmic rays and reflections from the spacecraft, before confirming the sightings in its preliminary report.

How big were the rocks?

Based on the brightness of the flashes, scientists estimate each rock was no more than a couple of inches wide, though moving thousands of miles per hour.

Why do these impacts matter?

Knowing how often small rocks hit the Moon helps NASA assess long-term risks to future habitats, equipment and astronauts on the lunar surface.

Can the public see the data?

Yes. More than 800 gigabytes of images, video, audio and annotated images are available through NASA's Planetary Data System.

Can people on Earth see lunar impact flashes?

item.title: NASA Welcomes Record-Setting Artemis II Moonfarers Back to Earth - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
The first astronauts to travel to the Moon in more than half a century are back on Earth after a record-setting mission aboard NASA’s Artemis II test flight.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen splashed down at 5:07 p.m. PDT Friday off the coast of San Diego, completing a nearly 10-day journey that took them 252,756 miles from home at their farthest distance from Earth.

“Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy, welcome home, and congratulations on a truly historic achievement. NASA is grateful to President Donald Trump and partners in Congress for providing the mandate and resources that made this mission and the future of Artemis possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Artemis II demonstrated extraordinary skill, courage, and dedication as the crew pushed Orion, SLS (Space Launch System), and human exploration farther than ever before. As the first astronauts to fly this rocket and spacecraft, the crew accepted significant risk in service of the knowledge gained and the future we are determined to build. NASA also acknowledges the contributions of the entire NASA workforce, along with our international partners, whose expertise and commitment were essential to this mission’s success. With Artemis II complete, focus now turns confidently toward assembling Artemis III and preparing to return to the lunar surface, build the base, and never give up the Moon again.”

After splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, the astronauts were met by a combined NASA and U.S. military team that assisted them out of the spacecraft in open water and transported them via helicopter to the USS John P. Murtha for initial medical checkouts. The crew members are expected to return to NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston on Saturday, April 11.

During their mission, Wiseman, Glover, Koch, and Hansen flew 694,481 miles in total. Their lunar flyby took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before, surpassing the previous distance record set by Apollo 13 astronauts in 1970.

The first Artemis crew launched on NASA’s SLS rocket at 6:35 p.m. April 1, from Launch Pad 39B at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. With 8.8 million pounds of thrust at liftoff, the American-built rocket propelled the crew inside the Orion spacecraft to space, delivering it to orbit with pinpoint accuracy after a smooth countdown conducted by the agency’s Artemis launch control team.

During the first day in space, the astronauts and teams on the ground checked out the spacecraft — named Integrity by the crew — to confirm all systems were healthy ahead of the transit to the Moon. NASA also deployed four CubeSats from international partners to Earth orbit.

On the second day of the test flight, with all systems Go, Orion’s service module fired its main engine, placing the astronauts on a trajectory that brought them 4,067 miles above the lunar surface at their closest approach.

“The Artemis II crew is home. The entry, descent, and landing systems performed as designed and the final test was completed as intended. This moment belongs to the thousands of people across fourteen countries who built, tested, and trusted this vehicle. Their work protected four human lives traveling at 25,000 miles per hour and brought them safely back to Earth,” said NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya. “Artemis II proved the vehicle, the teams, the architecture, and the international partnership that will return humanity to the lunar surface. Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy carried the hopes of this world farther than humans have traveled in more than half a century. Fifty‑three years ago, humanity left the Moon. This time, we returned to stay. The future is ours to win.”

With astronauts aboard for the first time, engineers put Orion through a full in‑flight evaluation. The crew tested the spacecraft’s life support systems, confirming Orion can sustain humans in deep space. During several piloting demonstrations, crew members took manual control of the spacecraft, flying Orion to validate its handling and collect data that will guide future rendezvous and docking operations with human-rated landers during Artemis III and beyond.

The crew completed a series of tests to inform how NASA will fly future missions to the Moon, including evaluations of how the spacecraft operates during crew exercise, emergency equipment and procedures, the Orion crew survival system spacesuits, and other critical spacecraft systems.

Wiseman, Glover, Koch, and Hansen also supported scientific investigations to help NASA prepare astronauts to live and work on the Moon as the agency builds a Moon Base and looks toward Mars. These experiments — including the AVATAR investigation, which studies how human tissue responds to microgravity and the deep space radiation environment, and other human research performance studies — are gathering essential health data for long-duration missions.

During their April 6 lunar flyby, the astronauts captured more than 7,000 images of the lunar surface and a solar eclipse, during which the Moon blocked the Sun from Orion’s vantage point. The imagery includes striking views of earthset and earthrise, impact craters, ancient lava flows, our Milky Way galaxy, and surface fractures and color variations across the lunar terrain.

They documented the topography along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night — where low-angle sunlight casts long shadows across the surface, creating illumination conditions similar to those in the South Pole region where astronauts are scheduled to land in 2028. The crew also proposed potential names for two lunar craters and reported meteoroid impact flashes on the night side of the Moon.

Artemis II science will pave the way for future missions to the Moon’s surface by helping advance mission operations and training astronauts to use well-informed judgment to identify areas of high interest for science and exploration.

With the crew safely on Earth, NASA and its partners now will turn attention to preparing for next year’s Artemis III mission, when a new Orion crew will test integrated operations with commercially built Moon landers in low Earth orbit.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly challenging missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and lay the groundwork for sending the first astronauts – American astronauts – to Mars.

To learn more about the Artemis program, visit:
